passage:
Manoj hadn't gone to cricket in two months. It started small: Siddharth didn't like him staying out late, so he came home earlier. Then Siddharth wanted his phone checked "just to feel safe." Then certain friends were "bad influence." Each time it came with the same line: "I only do this because I love you."

At the tea stall near the bus stand, his old friend Vinay stopped mid-sip. "You've vanished, yaar. You don't even laugh the same."

The words landed hard. Manoj went home and sat on his bed, looking at his own contact list, half the names hidden from him now by habit. Something was wrong, and it did not feel like love.

The next day he walked into the college counselling room, hands shaking, and said, "I need to tell someone what is happening."

qa.q: How long had Manoj stayed away from cricket?
qa.a: He had not gone to cricket in two months.

qa.q: What did Manoj feel when Vinay said he had vanished?
qa.a: The words landed hard and made him uneasy; he sat afterwards looking at his contact list and sensing something was wrong that did not feel like love.

qa.q: What did Manoj do that was a wise step, and why?
qa.a: He went to the college counselling room and told someone, because talking to a trusted person helps him see the pattern and is not a failing of his.

qa.q: How does Vinay see the change in Manoj?
qa.a: He sees a friend who has disappeared and stopped laughing the same way, and he cares enough to say so plainly.

grounding: Shows control framed as love slowly shrinking a person's world, with the person recognising the pattern and reaching out for help.

passage: By her second year at university in Manchester, Chidi had stopped going to the Nigerian society dinners. Siddiq said the guys there 'looked at her wrong'. She'd stopped wearing her yellow dress because he said it was 'for attention'. He checked her location 'because he loved her', and got upset if she took more than ten minutes to reply. Each rule came wrapped in a kiss or a worried face, so she told herself it was love. One afternoon her old flatmate Grace bumped into her in the library. 'Chidi! We never see you any more. Are you okay?' Chidi opened her mouth to say fine and, to her own surprise, started crying. Over coffee she listed the rules out loud and heard them properly for the first time. Grace said gently, 'That's not love, that's control. And it's not your fault.' That week, with Grace beside her, Chidi went to the university counselling service. She wore the yellow dress.

qa.q: What did Siddiq say about Chidi's yellow dress?
What did Chidi feel when Grace asked if she was okay?
qa.a: She was surprised by her own tears, feeling the weight of how small her life had become.

qa.q: What helped Chidi start to see the pattern?
qa.a: Listing the rules out loud to Grace, hearing Grace name it as control, and going to the counselling service.

qa.q: How does Grace see Siddiq's rules?
qa.a: As control, not love, and she makes sure Chidi knows it isn't her fault.

grounding: Shows a young woman whose partner's control is framed as love, recognising the pattern with a friend and seeking counselling; it is not her fault.

passage: In the hostel common room, Raghav noticed Tushar checking his phone again, the fourth time in ten minutes, and switching seats so his back was to the TV where students from the girls' block were watching cricket. 'Kriti doesn't like me sitting near other girls,' Tushar muttered. Over the semester he'd quit the band, skipped Raghav's birthday, and sent Kriti a photo every hour to prove where he was. 'She just loves me a lot,' he always said. That night Raghav said quietly, 'Bro, you've disappeared. This isn't what love looks like. It's control.' Tushar got defensive, then went silent. Then he admitted he felt like he was walking on eggshells all the time, and that he thought it was his fault for being 'bad at relationships'. 'It's not your fault,' Raghav said. The next morning Tushar sat in the student counselling centre's waiting room, Raghav beside him, filling in the form with shaking hands.

qa.q: How often did Tushar send Kriti a photo?
qa.a: Every hour, to prove where he was.

qa.q: How did Tushar describe feeling in the relationship?
qa.a: He felt anxious and tense, as if walking on eggshells all the time, and wrongly guilty for being 'bad at relationships'.

qa.q: What did Raghav do that helped?
qa.a: He named the pattern as control, told Tushar it wasn't his fault, and went with him to the counselling centre.

qa.q: How does Raghav see the changes in Tushar?
qa.a: He sees his friend disappearing, quitting the band and skipping birthdays, under control framed as love.

grounding: Shows a young man whose world has shrunk under a partner's control framed as love, recognising it with a friend's help and seeking counselling.
